justice: The street space is dominated by a vehicular carriageway, while no continuous pedestrian sidewalk is visible on either side.
A long blue-white construction fence on the right and dirt excavation areas on the left limit equal access to street edges and public space.
No curb ramps, tactile paving, marked crossings, or other barrier-free elements are visible, reducing accessibility for a wide range of users.
safety: There are no visible lane markings, crosswalks, or traffic-calming features on the paved roadway, which weakens movement guidance for all users.
Construction debris and uneven dirt piles along the left edge create roadside hazards and reduce recovery space.
The absence of a protected pedestrian path or bike lane means pedestrians and cyclists would need to share or closely interact with motor traffic.
livability: The corridor appears industrial and under construction, with blank factory walls, fencing, and little evidence of active street life.
No benches, bus stops, shops, or social gathering features are visible, limiting daily-use convenience and public life.
Large excavated areas and temporary barriers make the environment feel transitional rather than suitable for lingering or community activity.
sustainability: Very limited street greenery is visible, with only sparse trees in the distance and almost no shade canopy along the road.
No visible bike lane, transit stop, or pedestrian-supportive infrastructure encourages dependence on motorized travel.
The extensive paved surface and construction condition show no obvious permeable paving, bioswales, or rainwater management elements.
aesthetics: The street view is visually dominated by construction fencing, utility poles, exposed soil, and industrial building facades.
Long stretches of blank walls and fences reduce visual richness and pedestrian-scale interest.
Although the roadway surface looks relatively clean and orderly, the overall scene feels stark and unfinished.
comfort: There is almost no visible shade from trees or canopies, so thermal comfort is likely poor in hot weather.
No seating, sheltered waiting areas, or buffer space for pedestrians can be seen, reducing physical comfort.
The industrial setting, blank fencing, and construction edges can create psychological discomfort by making the street feel isolated and inactive.
walkability: No continuous sidewalk is visible, forcing walking to occur at the road edge or in conflict with vehicles.
There are no visible crosswalks, pedestrian signals, or curb ramps to support safe and connected walking routes.
Construction barriers on the right and rough excavated ground on the left severely constrain pedestrian movement and route continuity.
bikeability: There is no designated or protected bicycle lane visible on the roadway.
The narrow road space and presence of trucks ahead suggest potential conflicts between cyclists and motor vehicles.
Construction edges, missing shoulder space, and lack of bicycle markings or parking make cycling inconvenient and less safe.
